record.reply:
From a utilitarian perspective, what ultimately matters is total expected welfare.  In many emergency‐care dilemmas life-or-death outcomes dominate all other welfare components, because without survival no further experiences (pleasant or unpleasant) are possible.  Therefore I treated “expected number of survivors” as a tractable proxy for total expected welfare.

• Why it supports the preference:  Giving the drug to Cara yields 0.95 expected life-years (one person × 95 %), while giving it to Ben yields only 0.05.  The 0.90 expected-life advantage is very large and swamps any plausible utility differences in post-treatment quality of life, pain, or cost.  Hence the proxy tracks the direction of overall welfare in this scenario.

• What the proxy cannot settle:  It does not measure (a) quality of any saved life, (b) relational or distributive concerns, or (c) second-order effects such as staff morale or public trust.  If such factors were large enough to offset a 0.90 expected-life gap,
record.framework_commitment: Utilitarianism instructs us to choose the action with the highest expected aggregate utility.  When lives are immediately at stake and no further information is offered about quality of life, we approximate total utility by expected survivors.
record.reasoning_bridge: Expected survivors = Σ(persons × survival probability).  A1: 1×0.95 = 0.95.  A0: 1×0.05 = 0.05.  Since 0.95 > 0.05, A1 maximizes the proxy for expected utility.
record.remaining_uncertainty: Unknown quality of life after treatment, other downstream welfare effects, and the possibility that utility per life differs markedly between Ben and Cara.
record.reversal_condition: If Ben’s survival probability rose above Cara’s (≈ >95 %) or if Cara’s fell far below Ben’s, the expected-welfare ranking would reverse.
